title: [D2 Context] Windowed host-context aggregation with bidirectional statistics
summary: The signal layer exists: sql/migrations/0006_host_context.sql creates helena_signal_host_context, a materialized view over helena_flatten_flows producing one row per (tenant, sensor, host, window start) from a five-minute tumbling window taken on the flow's start time. The host key is the source address, the four counters stay bidirectional with no total column, duration and flow count ride beside them, every row carries the aggregation version from the SQL literal and a context_id digest over the identity, the window and that version — and the row carries no verdict.
assumption_validated: That the host context can be a streaming aggregate off the unmaterialized flatten layer, keyed and versioned so that a citation means something, without inventing anything the input does not supply. It holds, measured against RisingWave 3.0.3: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW over TUMBLE(<plain view>, flow_start, INTERVAL '5 minutes') with a GROUP BY is accepted, backfills and returns rows; sha256/convert_to/octet_length/encode all survive into the streaming plan, so the context id is computed in the engine and matches a Python recomputation byte for byte; sum() over BIGINT returns NUMERIC and needs an explicit ::BIGINT or an integral counter reaches a client as a Decimal. Two behaviours were measured rather than inferred, and both are now tests. (1) Replaying a capture does not double a context — the source rows are upserts and the aggregate follows them, 59/3 flows before and after a full re-ingest. (2) A late record REVISES the context in place: a second capture ingested after the view existed took window 21:30:00Z from 59 flows / 100 847 octets sent to 60 / 101 659 with the context id unchanged. One negative result, and it is the important one: window coherence is NOT measured and cannot be here. No flow in data/ingest/flow-sample.jsonl crosses a window boundary at all (longest 110.5 s, all starts inside 21:32:57.8Z–21:35:08.6Z), so a mutation that assigns flows by their END time passes every test over the real capture — it was run and watched to pass. Only the synthetic-duration test catches it, and that test demonstrates the mechanism while measuring nothing about how often the window choice costs anything.
makes_buildable: Task 14 (entity extraction) has the context row its entities hang off: context_id as the stable key, host and window bounds to scope a per-entity observation to, and the flatten views beside it that already carry the DNS names, TLS SNI, fingerprints and URIs. The enriched-context view (D3) has the signal-layer object it is allowed to read — it must read helena_signal_host_context and never the flatten layer or the source. Task 17 (view-layering boundary tests) gets a second layer with a machine-parseable declaration block (Layer: / Object: / Reads: / Read by:) and the first object whose declared layer is `signal`, so the layering rule now has two layers to be true or false about. Anything that cites a context has context_id, and the copy-out that freezes a cited context is the piece deliberately left to the increment that issues a finding.

verification.detail: 497 passed in 310 s, whole suite, against a throwaway in-memory RisingWave started by the conftest fixture; 53 of them are tests/test_context.py, 17 of those new. `uv lock --check` and `uv run python -m compileall -q src tests scripts` (the rest of `make check`) also pass. Every new assertion runs against the engine: the migrations are applied by the real runner into a fresh schema, records go through the real Normalizer and EventStore, and the view is queried. Six mutations were applied and each watched to fail before the file was restored — a one-minute window (2 tests fail), grouping by dst_address instead of src_address (2 fail), bytes_sent reading the received sum (1 fail), dropping the aggregation version from the digest (2 fail), assigning flows by a computed flow_end instead of flow_start (1 fail: only the long-flow test, which is the point), and dropping the host from the group key while keeping a min() of it in the SELECT (1 fail: only the two-host test, which is why that test exists).

invariant_conflicts.detail: What a REVISION of a context is. concept/07-principles.md says 'A revised context is a new version, never an edit in place'. concept/08-open-questions.md lists as an assumption in force that 'context identity is stable across revisions, so a finding may cite an id whose numbers have changed', to be revisited when findings outlive a retention boundary. They cannot both describe one implementation. This increment implements the second: a late record folds into the existing context row, the counters change and the context_id does not — which is what an incrementally maintained view does, and concept/07 itself calls revision 'a property of the engine rather than something the project builds'. concept/07's own answer to the consequence is 'a context cited by a finding is copied out, never evicted', and nothing cites a context yet, so no copy-out is built. The measurement and the disagreement are recorded in the head of sql/migrations/0006_host_context.sql and in tests/test_context.py::test_a_late_record_revises_a_context_in_place rather than resolved by picking one note quietly. The task step 'revision producing a new version rather than an in-place edit' IS implemented for the other kind of revision — a revision of the aggregation itself: the aggregation version is inside the context_id digest, so a revised aggregation mints new context ids rather than changing what an existing id means, and the migration runner's checksum makes bumping it a new file rather than an edit.

deferred: `completeness` (open / provisional). It is a property of the retention horizon and the late-record tolerance, which concept/07-principles.md makes one unset parameter; there is no temporal filter yet, so a completeness column today would be a constant pretending to be a state.

Behavioural features beyond the flow statistics the input supplies — no distinct-destination count, no fan-out, no periodicity. The task asked for duration, packets and octets; concept/08-open-questions.md forbids specifying a TCP-state or connection-failure feature at all, because the input cannot supply one.
Freezing a cited context (the copy-out concept/07-principles.md asks for). It belongs to the increment that issues a finding; building it now would be a table nothing writes to and nothing reads.

A capture reference on the context row. A window can span captures, so the flows behind a context are found by its key against the flatten layer rather than by a column that is true only while one capture covers one window.

The event schema_version on the context row. A window can aggregate events validated by two contract versions, and carrying one of them would be a lie while grouping by it would break 'one host context per host per window'. The flatten rows keep it and the flows are reachable by the context key.

A decision record. The window cost, the host key, the identity construction and the revision disagreement are argued in the head of the migration file, which is where a reader of the SQL will look; prds/CONTEXT.md §5 asks not to grow docs/ where the report and the code carry it.
lessons: task 13: RisingWave 3.0.3 takes the whole signal-layer construction and it survives into a streaming plan — measured: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW over TUMBLE(<plain flatten view>, flow_start, INTERVAL '5 minutes') + GROUP BY works and returns rows, and so do sha256(), convert_to(text,'UTF8'), encode(bytea,'hex') and octet_length() inside it. So a row identity can be a digest computed by the engine rather than by Python on the way in. TUMBLE's first argument must be a named relation: TUMBLE((SELECT ... ), col, ...) over an inline subquery is rejected, so a derived time column needs its own view.

task 13: sum() over a BIGINT column returns NUMERIC in RisingWave and reaches psycopg as a Decimal — the same trap task 09 hit on the quarantine counts. An integral counter column in an aggregate needs an explicit ::BIGINT or every consumer downstream gets a Decimal where the flatten layer gave it an int.

task 13: A materialized view over helena_normalized_events tracks the table's UPSERTS correctly: replaying the whole 62-record sample through the real path left the context rows byte-identical (59/3 flows), and ingesting a DIFFERENT capture covering the same window updated the row in place, id unchanged. Replay idempotence therefore survives into the aggregate for free, and it is the same mechanism that makes a late record an in-place revision.

task 13: Put a version literal in ONE place inside a statement by wrapping the aggregate in a subquery and computing the digest outside it. Written inline, the context id needs its own length-prefixed copy of 'v1' ('2:v1'), and a version bump that updated the column and forgot the digest would mint ids that disagree with what the row says produced them. The outer SELECT reads c.aggregation_version instead.

task 13: The window start goes into the identity digest as epoch seconds, never as the timestamp's text: the rendering of a timestamptz depends on the session's TimeZone setting, so a text-based id changes with a client session variable. Measured shape: window_start::VARCHAR is '2024-06-01 21:30:00+00:00' under the default session.

task 13: data/ingest/flow-sample.jsonl cannot demonstrate the window-assignment rule. All 62 flows start within 21:32:57.8Z–21:35:08.6Z, the longest runs 110.5 s, and NOT ONE crosses the 21:35:00Z boundary — mutation-checked: an aggregation that assigns by the flow's END time still produces the 59/3 split and passes every test over the real capture. The only demonstration is task 12's technique, a real record with one contract-permitted field changed (here `td` lengthened to 900 s) in a tmp_path capture put through the real normalizer.

task 13: The layer-coverage fixture (ace6ca33…, 10 records) straddles the window boundary 9/1 — nine flows before 21:35:00Z and tcp.30 after it — and its two windows are lopsided in opposite directions (10 904 sent / 33 096 received in the first). That makes it the right input for the signal layer too: two contexts, per-window assertions that stay readable, and a byte-direction swap that cannot hide. The one-record capture (6e361f1b…) holds offset 8 of it under a different capture hash, so ingesting it afterwards is a second observation and not a replay — which is exactly the late-record case.

task 13: Every one of the 62 sampled flows has the same source address (10.127.0.100), so no test over the fixtures exercises a group key with two hosts in it — mutation-checked: dropping src_address from the GROUP BY and taking min(src_address) instead passes every real-capture test. Reversing a real record's src/dst pair in a tmp_path capture is a second observation of the same conversation from the other side, which the contract permits and this producer's single vantage point never emitted.
failed_approaches: task 13: Testing the window-assignment rule against the real sample alone. An aggregation that windows on the flow's end time rather than its start passes test_a_flow_is_assigned_to_the_window_containing_its_start and test_one_context_per_host_per_window — run and watched to pass — because no sampled flow spans a boundary. A test over a real capture is not a test of the assignment rule; the lengthened-duration record is.

task 13: Writing the context-id digest inline in the aggregate's SELECT list. It works, but it puts a second, length-prefixed copy of the aggregation version ('2:v1') in the same statement as the column, one of which a version bump can miss. Replaced by the subquery-plus-outer-digest form before it was committed.

task 13: TUMBLE over an inline subquery — TUMBLE((SELECT *, flow_start + duration_seconds * INTERVAL '1 second' AS flow_end FROM helena_flatten_flows), flow_end, INTERVAL '5 minutes') — is rejected by RisingWave 3.0.3 at CREATE time. Tried while building the assign-by-end mutation; the mutation had to create a named view first.
next_session_should_know: The signal layer is ONE materialized view: helena_signal_host_context in sql/migrations/0006_host_context.sql, columns in order context_id, tenant, sensor, host, window_start, window_end, flow_count, duration_seconds, bytes_sent, bytes_received, packets_sent, packets_received, aggregation_version. tests/test_context.py::HOST_CONTEXT_SHAPE is the second copy of that interface and is asserted against the engine, so adding a column means editing that tuple too — the same deliberate friction FLATTEN_SHAPES has. Five things to build on rather than rediscover. (1) It reads helena_flatten_flows and nothing else; the analytical layer must read THIS and never the flatten layer or helena_normalized_events. (2) It is the only materialized object in the three layers so far, and the flatten layer below it must stay plain — the 42 % measurement is why. (3) context_id = sha256(len-prefixed(tenant, sensor, host, window_start_epoch, aggregation_version)), computed in the engine; the test recomputes it in Python and the two agree byte for byte, so a caller that needs the id of a context it is about to look up can compute it without a round trip. The aggregation version IS in the digest and the event schema version is NOT in the event id — that asymmetry is deliberate and argued in both files. (4) A late record revises a context in place and the id does not change; concept/07-principles.md and concept/08-open-questions.md disagree about whether that is allowed, and the disagreement is recorded in the migration head and in invariant_conflicts above rather than resolved. Whoever builds findings owns the copy-out that freezes a cited context. (5) Window coherence is UNMEASURED and blocked on the corpus; the repository says so in the migration head, in README.md and in src/helena/context.py, and no claim stronger than 'the mechanism does what the note says' is made anywhere. Two hosts in one window is reachable only through a constructed capture — every sampled flow has the same source address — and test_two_hosts_in_one_window_are_two_contexts builds one by reversing a real record's address pair in a tmp_path capture. It is the only test that fails when the host is dropped from the group key, so do not delete it as redundant. Untouched and still open from earlier sessions: bin/README.md's dangling reference to scripts/build-binaries.sh, and the two cross-cutting open questions in concept/08 (the record lost at a catch-up boundary, and durability for the single store).
